title: Effects of vaccination programmes on antibiotic consumption and antimicrobial resistance: a global scoping review

analysis.scope_and_question: This scoping review aimed to evaluate the effects of vaccination programmes on antibiotic consumption and antimicrobial resistance, specifically focusing on human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and related entities.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidance and was reported using PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S. PubMed was searched in June 2026 for records published from 1999 to 2025, with Europe PMC, WHO Global Index Medicus, Google Scholar and citation searching used as supplementary routes.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Vaccination can reduce antimicrobial resistance (AMR) by preventing infections that trigger antibiotic treatment, lowering transmission of resistant vaccine-targeted strains and reducing population antibiotic selection pressure. An investigational maternal respiratory syncytial virus vaccine reduced infant antimicrobial prescribing by 12.9%; rotavirus, COVID-19 and typhoid studies extended the pathway beyond influenza and pneumococcus.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Influenza vaccination generally reduced respiratory antibiotic exposure, although null trials and seasonal heterogeneity prevented a universal effect. Serotype replacement and ecological confounding limited inference for total AMR burden.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Vaccination is an upstream component of antimicrobial stewardship, with the strongest evidence for reduced influenza-associated prescribing and resistant vaccine-type pneumococcal disease. Vaccine programmes should be integrated with diagnostic and prescribing stewardship and sustained serotype, genomic and antimicrobial-consumption surveillance.

analysis.summary_en: This scoping review evaluates the impact of vaccination programmes on antibiotic consumption and antimicrobial resistance, focusing on human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and related entities. The review mapped global primary evidence published from 1999 to 2025, using PubMed and supplementary sources. It found that vaccination can reduce AMR by preventing infections that require antibiotic treatment, lowering transmission of resistant strains, and reducing population antibiotic selection pressure. The strongest evidence was for reduced influenza-associated prescribing and resistant vaccine-type pneumococcal disease. However, controversies include seasonal heterogeneity and ecological confounding. Research and practice implications suggest integrating vaccination with antimicrobial stewardship and maintaining surveillance of serotype, genomic, and antimicrobial-consumption data.

title: Pediatric RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection burden in G20 countries in 2023.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of childhood lower respiratory infections, but updated G20 burden estimates are lacking.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population.
analysis.methods: Using the Global Burden of Disease 2023 database, we analyzed deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) for RSV-associated lower respiratory infections in children aged 0-14 years across G20 members from 1990 to 2023, with stratification by sex, age, and country.
analysis.main_results: Infants aged <1 year bore the heaviest burden (mortality 8.688 per 100,000), and India ranked highest, whereas Australia ranked lowest.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Burden strongly correlated inversely with Sociodemographic Index.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings highlight the need for precision prevention, targeting the youngest children and lower-resource G20 members.

analysis.summary_en: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of childhood lower respiratory infections, but updated G20 burden estimates are lacking. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2023 database, we analyzed deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) for RSV-associated lower respiratory infections in children aged 0-14 years across G20 members from 1990 to 2023, with stratification by sex, age, and country. Infants aged <1 year bore the heaviest burden (mortality 8.688 per 100,000), and India ranked highest, whereas Australia ranked lowest. Burden strongly correlated inversely with Sociodemographic Index. These findings highlight the need for precision prevention, targeting the youngest children and lower-resource G20 members. title: A Confirmatory, Dual Center Nonhuman Primate Study on the Efficacy of Novel Oropharyngeal Spray Immunization With an Adenoviral Vector Vaccine Against RSV —Important Lessons Learned

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of a DNA prime—oropharyngeal adenoviral boost vaccination strategy against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.study_design_and_population: A randomized, blinded, dual center study was conducted across two European primate research facilities, involving rhesus macaques and including mock-vaccinated animals and a comparator group mimicking natural immunity induced by primary RSV infection.
analysis.methods: Rhesus macaques received an RSV fusion protein (F) DNA vaccine via electroporation, followed by two mucosal administrations of a recombinant adenovirus vector encoding the same antigen. Systemic and mucosal immune responses were monitored longitudinally.
analysis.main_results: Robust cellular and humoral immune responses were detected, but with some variability between the two centers. RSV-vaccinated animals demonstrated markedly reduced viral replication in the upper and lower respiratory tract after RSV challenge infection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The results support the potential of mucosal adenoviral boosting following DNA priming to induce protective immunity against RSV, while highlighting challenges associated with multi-center preclinical vaccine studies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of mucosal immunization strategies for RSV and underscore the importance of standardizing multi-center preclinical studies to ensure reliable vaccine efficacy assessments.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by unexpected RSV-specific immunity in the control group at one single study site, which prevented confirmation of the predefined primary endpoint. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of a DNA prime—oropharyngeal adenoviral boost vaccination strategy against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in a dual-center, randomized, blinded primate model. Rhesus macaques received an RSV fusion protein DNA vaccine via electroporation, followed by two mucosal administrations of an adenovirus vector encoding the same antigen. Systemic and mucosal immune responses were monitored over time. The results showed robust immune responses with some variability between centers, and vaccinated animals had reduced viral replication in the respiratory tract after challenge. However, unexpected immunity in the control group at one site prevented confirmation of the primary endpoint. The study highlights the potential of mucosal adenoviral boosting for RSV vaccines but also underscores challenges in multi-center preclinical trials. These findings have implications for vaccine development and the standardization of multi-center studies, though the evidence is moderate due to the unexpected control group immunity.
